lead: Small transformers and inductors need a high switching frequency, but every hard-switched transition burns energy while voltage and current overlap. Resonant converters place an inductor and capacitor around the switch and time the gate to the tank's zero crossings, so the device turns on at zero voltage or turns off at zero current. The loss per transition falls, the heatsink shrinks, and frequencies of hundreds of kilohertz become practical. You meet the idea in phone and laptop adapters, TV supplies and server power shelves.
prereq: You need: switching loss, output capacitance and heat sinks (see Switching losses, thermal design and heat sinks), and the PWM cells from Buck converter to Buck-boost and Cuk converters.

sections.h3: Hard switching sets a frequency ceiling

blocks.text: In a PWM converter the switch is told to change state while it holds the full load voltage and carries the full load current. For the short overlap time the device is neither off nor on: voltage falls while current rises, or current falls while voltage rises. That overlap is the hard-switching loss.

V is the off-state voltage, I the on-state current, t<sub>r</sub> and t<sub>f</sub> the turn-on and turn-off overlap times, f<sub>s</sub> the switching frequency. The ½ assumes that in each transition one quantity ramps linearly while the other holds its full value, as with an inductive load, so the overlap power is a triangle of height V·I.

Two more terms appear every cycle. A diode that turns off must sweep out its stored charge Q<sub>rr</sub>, costing about P<sub>rr</sub> = Q<sub>rr</sub> · V · f<sub>s</sub>, where Q<sub>rr</sub> is the reverse-recovery charge in coulombs (C). The device output capacitance C<sub>oss</sub> stores ½·C<sub>oss</sub>·V² and dumps it each cycle, costing P<sub>C</sub> = ½ · C<sub>oss</sub> · V² · f<sub>s</sub>, where C<sub>oss</sub> is in farads (F).

Conduction loss is separate: P<sub>cond</sub> = I<sub>rms</sub>² · R<sub>on</sub>, where I<sub>rms</sub> is the root-mean-square device current in amperes (A) and R<sub>on</sub> is the on-resistance in ohms (Ω). The total is P<sub>total</sub> = P<sub>cond</sub> + P<sub>sw</sub> + P<sub>rr</sub> + P<sub>C</sub>. At low f<sub>s</sub> the conduction term dominates and is roughly constant. Above some frequency the switching terms rise in proportion to f<sub>s</sub>, so P<sub>total</sub> has a minimum at a best frequency. Plain PWM pushed past that minimum gets hot faster than the magnetics shrink.

Soft switching moves the device transition to a zero. Zero-voltage switching (ZVS) turns the device on only after its voltage has fallen to zero. Zero-current switching (ZCS) turns the device off only after its current has fallen to zero. In both cases the voltage-current overlap is removed, so the ½·V·I·t term for that transition goes to zero.
L<sub>r</sub> and C<sub>r</sub> are the resonant inductance and capacitance; the tank swings energy at f<sub>0</sub>, and the switch is timed to its zero crossings.

For ZVS, a small resonant current flows before the gate pulse. It charges and discharges the device capacitance until the switch voltage reaches zero. Then the antiparallel body diode conducts and clamps the voltage at about zero. The gate pulse arrives while the diode is conducting, so the channel turns on with V ≈ 0. The body diode carries the current for that short wait.

For ZCS, the resonant inductor holds the current down. A resonant pulse brings the switch current to zero before the gate is removed. The device turns off with I = 0, and the voltage rises only afterwards. The price is a higher circulating current and a tank that must be tuned to the load.

A resonant converter replaces the PWM cell with a tank plus a switch. Four families cover most hardware. A series load-resonant converter puts the L-C tank in series with the load; the tank current is sinusoidal. A parallel load-resonant converter places the tank across the load; it can hold output at light load but carries more circulating current. A resonant-switch or quasi-resonant converter puts a small L<sub>r</sub> and C<sub>r</sub> around the switch, so the switch sees a zero crossing every cycle while the rest of the circuit still looks like a PWM cell. An LLC converter uses two inductors and one capacitor; it is common in laptop, phone and TV adapters because it gives ZVS on the primary switches.

The control variable changes. A buck sets V<sub>o</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub> with duty ratio D; a resonant converter sets its gain by the ratio f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>0</sub>. Above f<sub>0</sub>, raising f<sub>s</sub> lowers the gain; just below f<sub>0</sub> an LLC’s gain rises above 1 to a peak, and that region holds the output when the input sags. The gain curve also depends on the tank quality factor Q, so at light load the usable range shrinks. This makes the regulation range narrower than a buck's: an LLC may hold output over a 2:1 input range, not from 0 to V<sub>s</sub>.

Only a few universities derive the full gain curves. For most exams, know the loss comparison and the ZVS/ZCS definitions. If a paper asks for the gain, it usually gives the curve or asks for f<sub>0</sub> and the operating region.

spec.aria: Two panels with gate, voltage, current and power lanes over 200 nanoseconds. Left, hard turn-on: current rises to 5 amps while the voltage stays at 200 volts, then the voltage falls; the power triangle peaks at 1000 watts and holds 50 microjoules. Right, ZVS: the voltage falls to zero first, the body diode carries a small negative current, the gate then turns on and the current rises with zero voltage, so the power stays at zero.

examples.question: A MOSFET in a hard-switched converter blocks 200 V and carries 5 A. It switches at 100 kHz. The voltage-current overlap times are t<sub>r</sub> = 100 ns at turn-on and t<sub>f</sub> = 100 ns at turn-off, and the overlap is triangular. The on-resistance is 0.1 Ω. Take 5 A as the rms device current for conduction. (a) Find the switching loss. (b) Find the conduction loss. (c) The circuit is changed to ZVS, which removes the turn-on overlap but leaves the turn-off overlap. Find the new total loss and compare with the hard-switched total.
steps: Switching loss: P<sub>sw</sub> = ½ × V × I × (t<sub>r</sub> + t<sub>f</sub>) × f<sub>s</sub>. First V × I = 200 × 5 = 1000 W. Then t<sub>r</sub> + t<sub>f</sub> = 200 ns = 2×10⁻⁷ s. So P<sub>sw</sub> = ½ × 1000 × 2×10⁻⁷ × 1×10⁵ = 10 W.
Conduction loss: P<sub>cond</sub> = I² × R<sub>on</sub> = 5² × 0.1 = 25 × 0.1 = 2.5 W.
Hard-switched total: P<sub>total</sub> = P<sub>sw</sub> + P<sub>cond</sub> = 10 + 2.5 = 12.5 W.
With ZVS the turn-on overlap t<sub>r</sub> is removed. Only turn-off overlap remains: P<sub>off</sub> = ½ × V × I × t<sub>f</sub> × f<sub>s</sub> = ½ × 200 × 5 × 1×10⁻⁷ × 1×10⁵ = 5 W.
New total: P<sub>ZVS</sub> = P<sub>off</sub> + P<sub>cond</sub> = 5 + 2.5 = 7.5 W. The saving is 5 W, or 40 % of the hard-switched loss.
examples.answer: P<sub>sw</sub> = 10 W, P<sub>cond</sub> = 2.5 W, and after ZVS the total falls from 12.5 W to 7.5 W.

traps: Using V·I·t·f<sub>s</sub> without the ½ doubles the switching loss. The ½ comes from the triangular overlap, not from a duty ratio.
ZVS removes the turn-on overlap, not the conduction loss. The MOSFET still carries current, so I²R<sub>on</sub> stays.
ZCS is a turn-off condition. It does not make the switch carry zero current during the on-time, and it does not clamp the off-state voltage to zero.
The tank frequency is 1/(2π√(L<sub>r</sub> C<sub>r</sub>)), not 1/√(L<sub>r</sub> C<sub>r</sub>). Missing 2π gives an answer in rad/s.
A resonant converter's gain is not D·V<sub>s</sub>. Do not use the buck formula when the control variable is switching frequency.

quiz.q: Define zero-voltage switching (ZVS) and zero-current switching (ZCS) in one line each.
quiz.a: ZVS turns a device on only after its voltage has reached zero. ZCS turns a device off only after its current has reached zero.

quiz.q: Why does the total loss of a hard-switched converter have a minimum as switching frequency rises?
quiz.a: Conduction loss is set by current and R<sub>on</sub> and stays roughly flat. Switching loss, diode recovery loss and C<sub>oss</sub> loss grow with f<sub>s</sub>. Once the switching terms exceed the saving from smaller magnetics, extra frequency only adds heat. The total therefore bottoms out at a best frequency.

quiz.q: A MOSFET has V = 100 V, I = 4 A, t<sub>r</sub> = 50 ns, t<sub>f</sub> = 80 ns and f<sub>s</sub> = 200 kHz. Find the switching loss.
A resonant tank has L<sub>r</sub> = 10 µH and C<sub>r</sub> = 100 nF. Find f<sub>0</sub>.
In the ZVS panel of the figure the switch voltage reaches 0 V before the gate signal arrives. What brings it to zero, and why is this ZVS?
quiz.a: A resonant current charges and discharges C<sub>oss</sub> until the switch voltage reaches zero. The body diode then conducts and clamps the voltage near zero. The gate pulse arrives while the diode holds V ≈ 0, so the channel turns on without voltage-current overlap. That is ZVS.

quiz.q: Why is the regulation range of an LLC converter narrower than that of a buck converter?
quiz.a: The LLC gain is set by f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>0</sub> and the tank quality factor Q, not by duty ratio. Moving f<sub>s</sub> far from resonance lowers the gain and limits power. At light load Q is small and the gain curve flattens. A buck can use any duty from 0 to 1, but an LLC needs a frequency window and a tank designed for the load.

beyond: Not for the exam. LLC and series-resonant converters run at 100 kHz to over 1 MHz in phone chargers, TV supplies, server power and EV onboard chargers. Wide-bandgap GaN and SiC devices make those frequencies practical, and phase-shifted full-bridge designs use ZVS on the primary side. Search for LLC resonant converter gain curves, ZVS phase-shifted full bridge, and resonant switched-capacitor converters.
